title: Most Frequent Values Sum per Window
statement:
You get an integer array nums and two integers k and x. Slide a window of length k across nums. For each window, compute its top-x sum:

  • Count how many times each distinct value appears in the window.
  • Rank the distinct values by count, highest first. When two values have the same count, the larger value ranks higher.
  • Keep the top x values and add up every occurrence of them in the window. If the window has fewer than x distinct values, that is simply the sum of the whole window.

Return an array whose i-th entry is the top-x sum of the window starting at index i, for i from 0 to n − k.

examples.why: First window [2, 2, 5, 1]: 2 appears twice, then 5 and 1 tie at once and the larger 5 wins: 2 + 2 + 5 = 9. The next two windows keep 1 (twice) and 5: 1 + 1 + 5 = 7.
Only two distinct values, fewer than x = 3, so the whole window counts.
Frequency beats size: 3 appears twice in each window, so it ranks above 8. Both of its occurrences count, giving 6, not 3.

hints: Start with one window. How would you compute its top-x sum from a count of each value?
Turn the counts into (count, value) pairs and sort by count descending, then value descending. Take the first x pairs and add count × value for each.
Neighbouring windows differ by one value leaving and one entering. Update the counts instead of recounting, then rank again.

explain.intuition:
For one window the recipe is mechanical: count each value, sort the distinct values by (count, value) both descending, and add count × value for the first x of them. If there are fewer than x distinct values, the loop simply takes all of them, which is the whole window's sum, so that case needs no special code.

Moving to the next window only changes two counts: the value that falls off the left loses one, and the value that enters on the right gains one. Keeping a running count map is the standard sliding-window move. Here the ranking still needs a sort per window, which is fine for these sizes; the larger version of this problem replaces that sort with two balanced ordered sets.
steps: Build a count map for the first k values.
For each window: sort the map's entries by count descending, then value descending, and add count × value for the first x entries.
Before the next window, decrement the count of the value leaving on the left (deleting it at zero) and increment the value entering on the right.
Collect the sums in order and return them.
pitfalls: Breaking ties toward the smaller value. A tie in count goes to the larger value, as with 5 over 1 in the first example.
Adding each chosen value once instead of count × value.
Leaving zero-count entries in the map. They still sort and can take one of the x slots, which is harmless for the sum but wrong if you later report which values were picked.

solutions.title: Recount every window
solutions.idea: For each start index, count the window from scratch, rank the values and add up the top x.

solutions.title: Sliding count map
solutions.idea: Keep the counts up to date as the window moves, and only rank them per window.

followups: Now n is 100 000 and x can be large. How do two ordered sets (the top x and the rest) plus a running sum give O(log n) per step?
What if ties went to the value that entered the window most recently instead of the larger value?
